9.0.0.en: In this chapter we are told how the people did not preserve their gratitude to Gideon and his family. After Gideon's death, Abimelech went to his mother's family to stir up a rebellion against his seventy brothers, relying on the fact that he was of their bone and flesh, because his mother, that is, Gideon's concubine, belonged to a family of a Canaanite tribe. What drove him to this was his feeling that he would not inherit together with his seventy brothers because he was the son of a concubine, since the sons of concubines do not inherit with the sons of the free wives.

9.1.0.en: Shechem: it is the present-day Nablus (map 11). He asked the sons of his mother's clan to speak to the people of the city of Shechem so that they would accept him as their ruler, claiming that it was better for them that he alone should reign over them than that seventy rulers, the seventy sons of Gideon, should have dominion over them. He added to this that he was related to the people of Shechem on his mother's side, and therefore he was closer to them than his other brothers.

9.2.0.en: His maternal uncles and his mother's relatives responded to his request and were convinced by his arguments, and they spoke to the rest of the people of Shechem what Abimelech had said, and welcomed his idea, feeling that he was related to them by kinship, since his mother was one of them.

9.3.1.en: To show the loyalty of the people of Shechem and their support for Abimelech, they gathered seventy shekels of silver from the treasury of the pagan temple which they worshiped, called Baal-berith, and gave it to him to help him in his pursuit of rulership. Abimelech used this sum to hire some wicked men to be soldiers who would help him achieve his evil goal.

9.4.0.en: As soon as he had obtained the support of the people of Shechem, he went to Ophrah, the town of his father's clan, and seized his seventy brothers and killed them all, by putting the head of each one on the same stone and striking off his neck with the sword. Only one of the brothers, the youngest, whose name was Jotham, was able to escape and save himself from that massacre.

9.4.1.en: Thus the unfaithfulness of the children of Israel to Gideon and to his sons was shown, because no one opposed Abimelech or stood in his way as he killed the seventy sons of Gideon. So they helped the murderer who loved rulership to gain dominion over them; they sinned against God and helped him in evil.

9.5.0.en: The fortress: a tower in Shechem.

9.5.1.en: The people of Shechem and the lands around it agreed together to accept Abimelech as their ruler, and they went to him to enthrone him as king over them. Their allegiance was made at a famous oak called "the oak of the pillar," the one under which Jacob buried the images of the pagan gods (Gen 35:1-4), and beside which Joshua set up a stone to confirm the covenant between the people and God (Josh 24:26, 27). This is the first time that the name of a king is mentioned in Israel, but he was not a king over all the people like David and Solomon; he was a king over a small part of the people who dwelt in Shechem and the region around it.

9.5.2.en: Abimelech's reigning does not mean that he was the judge who came after his father Gideon, since God had not called him to that; besides, his aim was the love of rulership, not teaching the people God's commandments and judging for them. This event is recorded to show the danger of the love of rulership. On the contrary, it shows how humble his father Gideon was and how far he kept from the love of rulership.

9.5.3.en: Do not let your heart be attached to positions, for they pass away; besides, your attachment may drive you to use means that are against God's commandments. Rather let your aim be the love of God, and He will bless your life and your works and secure for you your peace and happiness on earth and then in heaven.

9.6.s.en: (2) Jotham rebukes the people of Shechem

9.6.0.en: Gerizim: the mountain at which the blessings were pronounced for those who obey God (Josh 8:30-33) (map 11). Jotham was very angry with the people of Shechem for killing his brothers, so he went up to Mount Gerizim, which overlooks the city of Shechem lying in the valley before it, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and called to its inhabitants to hear him, so that God might accept them and hear their requests. This was a wise beginning on his part, by which he drew them to listen to his words, because he spoke from the mountain of blessing; besides this, he began his speech with a parable to make them eager to hear his words. And from a mountain in the wilderness a voice can resound and be heard throughout the whole valley, and even on the opposite mountain as well.

9.7.0.en: "Anoint a king over us": set a king over them. It is said "anoint" because among the rites of setting up the kings of Israel was anointing them with the holy anointing (the holy oil). He gave them a parable from nature, saying that the trees decided to set a king over themselves, and they offered the kingship to the olive tree.

9.8.0.en: The olive tree refused the kingship, saying that it would not give up its good oil, with its many benefits, from lighting the lamps to making the holy anointing oil and adding it to delicious foods; it would not leave all this to exchange it for a passing greatness that no one benefits from. By this parable he declares that a man's work and his service to those around him are more important than his love of rulership, behind which stand pride and domination, as Abimelech did.

9.9.0.en: The trees turned to another useful tree, the fig tree, and offered it to reign over the rest of the trees, but it also refused, because it was not ready to leave its services to the people, giving them good, sweet-tasting fruit, in order to boast of the false greatness of kingship.

9.10.0.en: The wine: the juice of fresh grapes before it ferments.

9.10.1.en: The trees made the same offer to the vine, and it answered with the same reply as the other useful trees, namely that it would not leave the juice of the grape, which gladdens the hearts of men and is poured out upon the sacrifices, so that God is pleased with it and is well pleased with those who offer them.

9.11.0.en: When the trees found no response from the splendid, useful trees, they were compelled to offer the kingship to a tree that gives neither fruit nor shade, and is all thorns, the bramble, whose thorns they used as fuel because it catches fire quickly.

9.12.0.en: The bramble knew of the other trees' refusal of the kingship, and knew that resorting to it was not because of its worthiness. Therefore it challenged the other trees that if they truly wanted it as king over them, they should come and take refuge in its shadow. It said this knowing that it has no shadow for the trees to find shade in, and therefore it cannot protect them and is not fit to be a king over them. It added that if they were not able to take refuge in its shadow - and that is certainly the actual state of affairs - then strife would arise between them, because the trees would realize the bramble's uselessness to them and turn against it, and it would meet their turning with violence, for fire would come out from it and consume the trees, even the great ones among them, such as the cedar, known for the massiveness of its trunk and the height of its stem.

9.12.1.en: By this parable Jotham was pointing to the people of Shechem by the trees, and the useful trees and the cedars by the sons of Gideon whom Abimelech had murdered, and he points to the wicked Abimelech by the bramble, showing the foolishness of the people of Shechem in rallying around him and enthroning him as king over them. He also points to the slain sons of Gideon as being like the olive, the vine and the fig tree, who do not seek the love of rulership but serve those around them in quietness. As for Abimelech, he points to him as the bramble, unable to serve others because it has no shadow, but on the contrary harms those around it with its thorns and burns easily, so that it burns those around it, who are the people of Shechem who supported him. Here we see that a bad choice of leader harms both the people and the leader as well.

9.13.0.en: The people of Shechem committed two great errors: the first was making Abimelech king, and the second was their unfaithfulness and failure to preserve their gratitude to Gideon and his sons. So Jotham rebuked them in the form of a question, which he answered at the end of his speech (v. 20). He asks them whether making Abimelech king was just and was done on the basis of a worthiness they found in him, and he asks them whether by this conduct of theirs they had preserved the gratitude owed for what Gideon had done for them.

9.14.0.en: He reminds them of what Gideon did in his wars to rescue the children of Israel from the oppression of their enemies the Midianites, and of the dangers he bore to secure for them freedom and safety.

9.15.0.en: The people of Shechem did not object to Abimelech's deeds in killing the seventy brothers, the sons of Gideon, and did not rebuke him for his evil work; rather they flattered him and swore allegiance to him as king, though he is not the son of a free wife but the son of a maidservant, and thus has no right to inherit his father, neither in wealth nor in authority.

9.16.0.en: Jotham shows his intense contempt for what the people of Shechem did to Gideon and his household, in a manner that makes light of their conduct, for he says to them that if what they did toward the house of Gideon was a just deed, then happy they are with Abimelech as king.

9.17.0.en: But if it was not a just deed but an unjust one - as is in fact the case - then their deed will turn against them, and the fire of strife and wars will be kindled between them and Abimelech, so that many of them will die, and Abimelech will die in it also.

9.17.1.en: What Jotham said was indeed fulfilled, as will come in the following verses.

9.18.0.en: After Jotham delivered his speech, which radiated bitterness and boldness at the same time, he fled so that Abimelech would not find him and strike him down as he had done before to his seventy brothers. He fled to a place called "Beer," which lies between Shechem and Jerusalem.

9.18.1.en: Be brave and proclaim the truth so that the wicked may take heed and turn back from their sins, taking care not to go beyond the proprieties of speech, and let your intention be the salvation of others and not merely anger on your part or any personal purpose or interest; and precede your speech with prayer, so that the words may be from God and by His power.

9.19.s.en: (3) The treachery of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech

9.19.0.en: With all the evil that Abimelech did, and his plotting against his brothers and killing them out of greed to be alone in rulership over Israel, he enjoyed the kingship for only three years, after which events and rebellions occurred that overthrew his kingdom and even his life, as the recompense for his wicked, unlawful ways and his shedding of innocent blood. And when it is mentioned that he ruled over Israel, the meaning is not all the tribes but a part of them, namely the tribe of Manasseh and some of the tribes surrounding it.

9.20.0.en: God allowed Satan to spread a spirit of hatred and division between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, so his recompense was of the same kind as his deed: as he betrayed his brothers, the people of Shechem betrayed him.

9.20.1.en: He who founds his life on injustice is destined to fall; a friendship built on self-interest and corrupt aims is destined to turn into enmity and hatred; and every gain or position that its owner obtains by unlawful means is destined to vanish, and its owner's end is destruction.

9.21.0.en: God used Satan to punish through him Abimelech and the people of Shechem for their injustice toward the sons of Gideon whom Abimelech had killed, for God's justice must be accomplished, and He repays each one according to his work.

9.22.0.en: The result of the spirit of hatred that crept into the hearts of the people of Shechem toward Abimelech was that they thought of a way to rid themselves of him, so they set some of their own men as lookouts on the roads in the mountains around the city of Shechem to play the part of highwaymen and rob the travelers, so that security would be disturbed and the people would rise against Abimelech for his inability to keep security, and news of those ambushes reached Abimelech. Perhaps they aimed to provoke him so that he would go out to investigate the matter and restore security, and they would kill him.

9.23.0.en: During those events a new adversary of Abimelech appeared, "Gaal the son of Ebed," who coveted seizing the kingship, and saw that the disturbances taking place might cause the people to gather around him because of their aversion to Abimelech's rule, and that the time was suitable to revolt against him. So "Gaal" came to Shechem, and what he had expected came to pass, for the people of Shechem rallied around him, trusted him, and supported him in his endeavor.

9.24.0.en: The time coincided with the gathering of the fruit, so the people of Shechem performed a pagan religious rite as a beginning for carrying out their plan against Abimelech. They went out into the field and gathered their vineyards and trod the grapes in the winepresses, and then made a glorification for their gods and praised them inside the temple of "Baal-berith," their god, and they ate and drank in the temple (the temple of Baal), and prayed to their gods that Abimelech might be cursed by those gods, so that it would be made easy for them to gain the victory in their war against him.

9.24.1.en: The rite of the glorification of the saints still remains among the rites of the Church to this day. But how great is the difference between those who glorify the saints in order to follow their life, their striving and their holding fast to their faith in the hardest situations, and to ask for their blessings and their intercessory prayers, and how vast is the difference between their holy glorifications and the glorifications of the pagans, whose aim was worldly merriment, during which they practiced drunkenness and debauchery as worship of their gods.

9.25.0.en: "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?": what is meant here is to exalt the standing of the people of Shechem and to remind them of their lofty position when compared with the lowly Abimelech, who does not deserve to be served by an ancient people such as the people of Shechem.

9.25.1.en: "Gaal" began to incite hatred of Abimelech and revolt against him, describing him as a lowly person unworthy of ruling over them, for the people of Shechem are too lofty to submit to Abimelech; he is the son of Gideon, who tore down the altar of Baal which they worship, so how can they make king a man who fought their worship? Likewise he described Zebul" l," Abimelech's officer, as incompetent and unworthy of the position of deputy of a king. He added to that that the ones more entitled to the kingship were the descendants of Hamor, the founder of the city, and not this stranger, the son of a concubine. "How, then, is it right for us to obey Abimelech and submit to his rule, when he is a man without integrity and an evil murderer?"

9.26.0.en: "If the people respond to me and obey me, I shall be able to overthrow the rule of Abimelech." Then "Gaal" sent a message to Abimelech, mocking him and challenging him, and inviting him to increase the number of his soldiers as much as he wished and come out to face him.

9.27.0.en: Abimelech had appointed "Zebul" as ruler of the city of Shechem and his officer there, while he himself dwelt in the town of "Arumah" (v. 41). What "Gaal" had said reached "Zebul's" ears, and he pretended to agree with his conduct while hiding something else inside himself, for he was angry at what "Gaal" had said and done, and was in truth working for the benefit of his master Abimelech.

9.28.0.en: Tormah: it is Arumah (v. 41), which lies 16.5 km northeast of Shechem (Nablus) (map 10). "Zebul" secretly sent messengers to Abimelech at "Tormah" to tell him what had happened, of the arrival of "Gaal" in the city of Shechem and his stirring up its people against Abimelech.

9.29.0.en: "Zebul" was a loyal officer to Abimelech, so he drew up for him a successful plan to confront "Gaal," asking him not to enter the city but to lie in wait by night in the fields, where he would hide until morning, when "Gaal" and his men would come out at the gates of the city and would be exposed, with no fortifications to shelter in; then he could surprise "Gaal" and his helpers and defeat them utterly and do to them whatever he pleased.

9.30.0.en: Abimelech lay in wait in the fields by night as "Zebul," his officer, had advised him, after dividing his army into four companies in preparation for fighting "Gaal" and those of the people of Shechem who followed him.

9.31.0.en: "Gaal" went out - as Zebul had expected - in the morning to take up his position at the entrance of the city, to defend it and to prevent Abimelech's army from entering it. Then Abimelech came out of his ambush to begin the battle according to a plan he had drawn up beforehand, as will come in the following verses.

9.32.0.en: Abimelech's men began to come down from the tops of the mountains surrounding the city, and Gaal saw them, and wanting to verify what he had seen, he asked "Zebul" whether he saw what he himself saw (and "Zebul," as we have already explained, was pretending to support Gaal while in truth he was obstructing his plan for the benefit of his master Abimelech). So "Zebul" deceived Gaal by saying that what he saw were not men but the shadows of the mountains as they appear in the early hours of the morning, so that the onlooker thinks they are persons.

9.33.0.en: The soothsayers: those who practice augury, which was originally scaring a bird so that it would fly, and people would see the direction in which it flew and take it as an evil or a good omen.

9.33.1.en: Gaal looked again and saw the men coming down from the mountains increasing more and more, and saw one of the companies coming from another direction, the way of the oak of the soothsayers, those occupied with knowledge of the unseen. This shows that Abimelech's dividing of his army into four companies was for the purpose of attacking his enemies from more than one side in order to confuse them. Gaal went back to assure Zebul that they were companies coming for war.

9.34.1.en: When the companies drew near to face Abimelech and his army, "Zebul" realized that "Gaal" had become entangled, so he ended his pretense of supporting "Gaal," and the truth of his alliance with Abimelech appeared. He said, "You are speaking empty words, and you have no power to face Abimelech. Are not the soldiers whom you see coming against you from every direction the soldiers of Abimelech, whom you despised and made light of, however many they are? So now show us your courage and your abilities, and go forward to fight him, if you can."

9.35.0.en: Gaal found no escape from the confrontation, so he went out at the head of his supporters, who had followed him from among the people of Shechem, to fight Abimelech.

9.36.0.en: The battle took place and Gaal was defeated and fled, after many of his men had fallen and their corpses covered the battlefield, reaching as far as the gate of the city of Shechem.

9.37.0.en: "Abimelech" came out of the war victorious and returned to the city which he had chosen as his place of residence, Arumah, near Shechem. "Gaal" and the remnants of his army had fled from before Abimelech's army into the city of Shechem, but Zebul, Abimelech's officer, drove them out of it so as to be safe from their starting a new rebellion in the future.

9.37.1.en: Do not rush into threats that are not calculated and that you are not able to carry out, and be deliberate in your speech so that it may have value and others may respect you, and so that all your decisions may be practical, and then people will love you and trust you.

9.38.s.en: (5) Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns the stronghold

9.38.0.en: After the revolt of "Gaal" against "Abimelech" was put down, the people of Shechem thought that matters had settled, so they went out to their fields to do their usual daily work. But Abimelech did not look at the matter in the same way. Although he had returned to his residence in Arumah, his heart had not become clear toward the people of Shechem, who had betrayed him and supported "Gaal" against him, so as soon as he learned that the people of Shechem had gone out to their usual work, he began to plan how to destroy them.

9.39.0.en: Abimelech gathered his army again and divided it into three companies, and went to the region surrounding the city of Shechem and lay in wait outside it until the people of the city went out to their work, and then he fell upon them and struck them according to a plan he had drawn up, the details of which will come in the following two verses.

9.40.0.en: The details of the plan he had drawn up were that he himself would lead one of the three companies into which he had divided his army, and its task would be to kill everyone who tried to go out to his work and everyone who returned from his work to the city. As for the other two companies, their task was to kill everyone they found outside the city in the fields.

9.41.0.en: "Sowed it with salt": he sprinkled salt on its farmland so that it would remain barren and not be sown afterward. This expression may mean the ruin of the city and the lands around it.

9.41.1.en: The next stage in the plan he drew up and carried out was that, after he had finished off those outside and inside the city and those beyond it, he stormed the city and fought against it all day and took it and killed those in it and laid waste its land so that it would not be sown afterward.

9.42.0.en: The stronghold of the house of El-berith: a high fortress attached to the temple of Baal-berith, which the people of Shechem worship, a fortress adjoining the tower of Shechem.

9.42.1.en: The reaction of the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem to what had happened in their city was to take refuge in the fortress of "the house of El-berith" attached to the citadel, which is more strongly fortified than the tower of Shechem, to fortify themselves in it and resist from it Abimelech's attack on their city.

9.43.0.en: Mount Zalmon: a part of Mount Gerizim near Shechem, full of trees.

9.43.1.en: Abimelech learned that the people of Shechem had fortified themselves in the tower, so he began to draw up a plan to seize it. He took his army and went up to Mount Zalmon and cut with his axe a bough from the branches of the trees that cover the mountain, and commanded his men to do likewise, and they did so, and each soldier carried a bough on his shoulder, and they laid them around the stronghold and set fire to them, and everyone who was in the stronghold and its tower died, burned or suffocated by the smoke, and the number of the dead was a thousand persons.

9.43.2.en: Do not support the wicked, lest harm befall you and God punish you for your encouragement of evil. Be strong, and if you do not rebuke evil, at least do not encourage it, so that perhaps the wicked may repent and so that you may save yourself from God's punishment.

9.44.0.en: After Abimelech took Shechem and subdued its people, he continued his campaign against another city that had joined Shechem in its revolt against his rule, the city of "Thebez," which lies 10 miles northeast of Shechem; he and his soldiers entered it and took it.

9.45.0.en: As usual, to shelter from the enemy soldiers, all the people of the city, men, women and children, took refuge in the stronghold in a strongly built tower erected in the middle of the city, and went up to the safest place in the tower, which is its top, and from it they could also watch the movements of the enemy army.

9.46.0.en: Abimelech tried to attack the tower and take it in the same way he had done in his attack on the stronghold of Baal-berith, so he drew near to the door of the tower in order to burn it with fire.

9.47.1.en: As he drew near to the door to burn it with fire, a woman cast a piece of a millstone, with which grain is ground, upon his head, and broke his skull.

9.48.0.en: Abimelech felt that he was close to death, so he commanded his young man, the bearer of his sword and his weapons of war, to draw the sword and kill him, lest the shame of dying at the hand of a woman attach to him; and the young man obeyed and carried out his master's command.

9.49.0.en: With the destruction of Abimelech, the members of the army that had rallied around him were scattered, as were all who had supported him in his wars, and each one went his own way.

9.50.0.en: This was the just judgment of heaven upon the great evil that Abimelech had done in killing without right his brothers, the seventy sons of Gideon; it was also a fulfillment of the saying of the Lord of glory in the Gospel, "All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."

9.50.1.en: The Lord may be patient with the wicked and warn them once and twice, but if the wicked take advantage of His longsuffering to persist in their evil, God will not leave them to corrupt the earth but will bring upon them the fitting punishment. But if they respond to the call of wisdom and turn back from their injustice, God forgives them. And in the Holy Bible we have many events that confirm this meaning, such as the story of Jonah and the people of Nineveh.

9.51.0.en: Abimelech had partners in the evil that he did, for which the Lord punished him: the people of Shechem, who supported him at the beginning and agreed with him in what he did, so their punishment too was a repayment of their evils upon them. Thus the curse of which Jotham had warned them in his speech was fulfilled, and the fire of hatred and wars came out between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and burned their fortresses with those in them, and in the end it burned Abimelech himself.

9.51.1.en: The judges Tola and Jair, then the enslavement of the people of God
